new_statements.rule_in_words: Santandrea treats Ngala, like the other Banda- and Zande-group languages in the book, as a tone language with lexically and grammatically significant tone (acute = high, grave = low; Ngala examples such as 'dì gùlá rí' are tone-marked). No rule for the position of word stress is visible; the only use of 'stress' seen is a phonetic note that in the diphthong oa 'all the stress' lies on the second vowel, which is about syllabification of a vowel sequence, not word accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None visible; the snippets are truncated.
new_statements.domain_note: The tone statement is a blanket statement for 'all these languages' (Banda, Golo, Gabu, Ngala, Zande, Nzakara, Pambia, Barambu), not specific to Ngala; it comes from Google Books snippet view, not from an opened page, so the page number and surrounding text are unverified. Words-in-isolation (lexical tone) and in-context (grammatical tone) are both discussed per the snippet.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ngal1296 'Ngala-Santandrea' (no ISO code) is the Ngala or Ngara of the Sopo and Boro rivers, western Bahr el Ghazal (refugees from what is now CAR), a Zande-group Ubangian language 'standing half-way between Banda and Zande' (Santandrea); about 30-50 speakers in the 1950s, presumably extinct. Not to be confused with Bantu Bangala/Lingala (ngal1301 is a different entry) nor with any other 'Ngala'. Santandrea 1965 groups it with Golo (NOCODE_Golo), Gabu (Gobu gox), Zande (zne), Nzakara (nzk), Pambia (pmb), Barambu (brm) and Banda-Dukpu (bjo); any statement in that book must be checked for whether it is about Ngala specifically or 'all these languages'.

sources.note: The only linguistic description of Ngala in existence (Glottolog: 'data appears in Santandrea 1965'; Grambank's sole source). Has a phonology part with §10 'Tones' and a comparative phonetic section where any stress/accent remark would sit; Santandrea's other outlines typically carry an explicit accent paragraph. Snippet view shows it is tone-marked; a full read is needed to confirm whether it says anything about word stress for Ngala specifically.
